Seniors shouldn’t wait half a decade for Medicare to cover FDA-approved breakthroughs while bureaucrats drag their feet. The Ensuring Patient Access to Critical Breakthrough Products Act tackles this by mandating a 4-year transitional coverage period (S.1717), forcing CMS to make timely coverage decisions. But let’s be real—this delay isn’t accidental. It’s systemic bloat.

Medicare’s TCET program caps nominations at five devices a year, creating artificial scarcity while patients suffer. Stanford’s data proves it: 56% of post-FDA-authorized tech still lacks coverage years later.

Streamlining this process isn’t just common sense—it’s a fiscal necessity. Every delayed device means higher long-term costs from untreated conditions and missed preventive care. CMS must prioritize efficiency over red tape.

The numbers don’t lie—see how bureaucratic inertia is costing lives and dollars: https://t.co/V3h1XE5eTX

Expanding Medicare coverage for breakthrough devices sounds noble, but H.R. 5343’s $10M annual CMS funding and four-year coverage window reek of corporate welfare disguised as innovation. Big Pharma’s FDA-approved “breakthroughs” often come with monopoly pricing—Medicare patients get temporary access, but taxpayers foot the bill for therapies that’ll cost 10x more once permanent coverage kicks in.

The bill’s Section 4 lets manufacturers lobby for designation while bureaucrats rubber-stamp “undue risk” exemptions. This isn’t about patient care—it’s about locking in profit pipelines before cost controls emerge.

Real reform would cap prices on taxpayer-subsidized treatments, not guarantee corporate paydays through Medicare’s checkbook.
